approachQuestion.prompt:
Display Ornament

A mutable character array text contains uppercase English letters and ASCII punctuation characters. Reverse the order of the letters while leaving every punctuation character at its original index. Return the same array. Do not resize it; all characters are single bytes.

Constraints: 0 <= n = text.length <= 200000. A letter is exactly A through Z; every other allowed character is punctuation.

Example 1: "A-BC!D" -> "D-CB!A".
Example 2: "?!" -> "?!".
Example 3: "AB" -> "BA".
constraints: Choose the most efficient valid approach for the entire stated input domain; accept equivalent optimal variants.

options.text: Move indices inward from both ends, skipping punctuation independently. When both point to letters and left<right, swap the letters and advance both.
options.feedback: Only letters are swapped, and each outermost remaining letter is paired with the corresponding letter from the opposite end.

options.text: Copy all letters into a buffer, then scan text left to right and replace each letter position with the next letter from the buffer read backward.
options.feedback: This reverses the eligible sequence correctly, but an endpoint scan can pair those positions without retaining the letters.

options.text: Reverse the entire array, then leave it as the result.
options.feedback: For "A!B?", it moves punctuation to new indices, producing "?B!A" instead of "B!A?".

options.text: For each i in the left half, swap text[i] with text[n-1-i] only when both are letters; otherwise skip that pair.
options.feedback: For "AB!C?", it skips A against ? and swaps B with C, producing "AC!B?" instead of "CB!A?". Eligible positions need not occur at equal distances from the ends.

feedback.reason: Coordinate endpoint scans over eligible positions while proving that ineligible positions never move.
details: Scan inward independently from both ends until both indices identify letters. Swap those two letters if their indices differ and advance both. Stop when the indices meet or cross. Never write to punctuation positions.

Punctuation positions stay fixed; only letters exchange places. Skipping nonletters independently at both ends finds the next actual pair without building a filtered copy or moving punctuation with it.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n is the byte length. Indexed character tests and swaps are constant time. No copied strings, buffers, recursion, hashing, or amortized operations.
constraints: Analyze this fixed method regardless of your answer to question 1; choose the tightest pair.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Inward indices inspect each character at most once.
details: Each endpoint advances across each position at most once, so the total work is linear and can require examining every character. The method retains only two indices and a character temporary.

Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n is the byte length. Indexed character tests and swaps are constant time. No copied strings, buffers, recursion, hashing, or amortized operations.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This adds an input-sized buffer absent from the fixed method.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This counts repeated full scans that the fixed method does not perform.
“O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The fixed method does not perform sorting or independent binary searches.
